title: NESTOR nested-precision brain: levels, precision ladder and tiers, per-cell precisions, sizes and clocks

items.text: A cell C is a tuple C = (M, pi, tau, G, I_in, I_out, {C_k}_k, Lambda): M is the cell's model type (spiking, LTC, SSM, ...), pi its precision profile (one format per tensor role), tau its native timescale and clock policy, G its geometric embedding, I its typed input/output ports, {C_k} its child cells (possibly empty), and Lambda its ledger: the observability record every cell must emit.

Micro (units and motifs). Individual neurons, synapses and small motifs of 1–100 units: a spiking neuron with STDP, an LTC cell, a ternary perceptron, a Clifford rotor unit, a fractional-order integrator. The micro level is where most parameters live, so it is where low precision pays the most.

Meso (circuits and organs). Circuits of 10^2–10^5 units that perform one function: a central pattern generator, a reservoir 'retina', a Mamba-style sequence summariser, a Hopfield episodic store, a homeostatic integrator. Each meso cell has one dominant model type and a precision profile.

Macro (the organism and its society). The whole brain: arbitration, global neuromodulation, the world model, the body schema, and (optionally) the links between organisms in a population. The macro level holds few parameters but long-lived, error-intolerant state, so it often warrants the highest precision.
Levels are relative, not absolute: a meso cell may itself be a complete NESTOR brain (brains within brains), and an entire organism may be one micro cell in a colony-level brain.

Why nested: an A-Life organism has to do many different things on many different timescales at once: reflexes in milliseconds, locomotion rhythms in tenths of a second, foraging plans over minutes, homeostasis and 'mood' over hours, development and learning over a lifetime.

Why mixed precision: precision is a resource, like energy or wiring length; in an A-Life setting, where many organisms must run in parallel on modest hardware, allocating precision well is the difference between a population of ten and a population of ten thousand.
MACRO: organism brain (arbiter + world model + homeostasis) — contains the meso cells below; any cell may itself contain a full sub-brain.
Sensory reservoir (LSM): analog / stochastic FP8; tau ~ 1 ms.
sLTC motor CPG: event-driven sLTC, ternary w. (weights); INT8 state, tau adaptive.
LTC / CfC controller: BF16 + FP32 tau-params; tau ~ 20–200 ms.
Mamba summariser: FP8 E4M3 / BF16 scan; event-driven.
World model (RSSM): BF16, posit16 latents; imagination clock.
Homeostat + mood: FP64 integrators; tau ~ minutes–hours.
Hub / sphere core routes global traffic between sub-brains over tokenless S2S channels.
DSD service: canonical motif library (shared, hash-consed).
Self-rewrite governor: propose -> sandbox -> verify -> commit / rollback; mediates every change to weights and biases.
Observability bus: every cell emits its ledger Lambda (states, spikes, gates, precisions, rewrites, DSD merges) -> Parquet / HDF5 / Zarr / NWB.

NESTOR treats numeric format as a per-tensor, per-role, per-time decision; the ladder runs from noisy analog and event codes at the bottom to FP64 and beyond at the top; 'bits' are per stored value, excluding shared scale metadata where block formats apply. Default zones: bulk micro weights, activations and signals, meso compute, slow error-intolerant macro state; the modifiers cut across rungs; the adaptive allocator moves tensors up and down the ladder at run time.
Precision ladder rung 1 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): Analog conductance — noise is the precision; effective 4–8 bits; in-memory compute.
Precision ladder rung 2 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): Spike timing / event code — information in when, not how much; precision set by clock resolution.
Precision ladder rung 3 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): Stochastic bitstream — value = probability of a 1; precision grows with stream length.
Precision ladder rung 4 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): Binary {-1,+1} (1 bit) — sign-only reflexes, hashing, HDC bipolar vectors.
Precision ladder rung 5 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): Ternary {-1,0,+1} (1.58 bit) — BitNet b1.58 style weights: add/subtract/skip.
Precision ladder rung 6 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): INT2 / INT3 — bulk sensory weights after DSD sharing.
Precision ladder rung 7 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): INT4 / NF4 — weight storage; NF4 matched to normal-shaped weights.
Precision ladder rung 8 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): FP4 E2M1 / MXFP4 / NVFP4 — NVFP4: FP8 scale per 16 values + FP32 tensor scale.
Precision ladder rung 9 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): MXFP6 (E2M3 / E3M2) — block-scaled middle ground.
Precision ladder rung 10 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): INT8 / Q8 (per-channel scale) — activations, spike counters, fixed-point membrane.
Precision ladder rung 11 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): FP8 E4M3 — forward activations and weights.
Precision ladder rung 12 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): FP8 E5M2 — gradients and wide-range signals.
Precision ladder rung 13 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): posit8 / LNS8 — tapered or log-domain: multiplies become adds.
Precision ladder rung 14 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): FP16 (IEEE half) — general compute; narrow range needs loss scaling.
Precision ladder rung 15 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): BF16 — default meso compute: FP32 range, 8-bit mantissa.
Precision ladder rung 16 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): posit16 / LNS16 — latents near ±1 get extra resolution.
Precision ladder rung 17 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): TF32 (19-bit compute) — tensor-core matmul with FP32 accumulate.
Precision ladder rung 18 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): FP32 — time constants, master weights, optimizer state.
Precision ladder rung 19 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): posit32 — alternative to FP32 for accumulators.
Precision ladder rung 20 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): FP64 — homeostasis, long-horizon integrators, audit replay.
Precision ladder rung 21 of 21 (1 = bottom: cheaper, denser; 21 = top: more bits, range, fidelity): double-double / FP128 — reference runs, chaos checks only.
Ladder modifier: stoch. rounding, Kahan — apply to any rung; unbiased low-bit updates.
Ladder modifier: per-component multivector — scalar / vector / bivector parts on different rungs (Sec. 5).
Precision tier column 1 of 6 in the hybrid grid (model type x precision tier): Analog / stochastic.
Precision tier column 2 of 6 in the hybrid grid (model type x precision tier): 1–1.58 bit.
Precision tier column 3 of 6 in the hybrid grid (model type x precision tier): 2–4 bit.
Precision tier column 4 of 6 in the hybrid grid (model type x precision tier): 8 bit (INT8, FP8, posit8, LNS8).
Precision tier column 5 of 6 in the hybrid grid (model type x precision tier): 16 bit (FP16, BF16, posit16).
Precision tier column 6 of 6 in the hybrid grid (model type x precision tier): 32–64 bit.

Model-type rows of the hybrid grid: sLTC / spiking; LTC / CfC; Reservoir / LSM; SSM / Mamba; World model; Clifford / geometric; Hopfield / HDC; NCA / PDE cells; ODE / DDE / fractional. A recipe appears in several cells because it is a hybrid; empty cells are open design space; the arrow shows R8's developmental annealing from high to low precision.

Principle: precision follows sensitivity times lifetime. A tensor deserves more bits when (a) the organism's behaviour is sensitive to small errors in it and (b) those errors accumulate over its lifetime instead of being washed out.

Precision demand D(theta) = E[ ||grad_theta L|| ] * sigma_q(theta) [first-order sensitivity] x T_life(theta) / tau_wash(theta) [accumulation], where sigma_q is the quantisation noise at the current rung, T_life is how long the value persists, and tau_wash is how fast downstream dynamics forget perturbations; L may be a task loss, a homeostatic error, or divergence of behaviour from a high-precision shadow run.
Static default 1: Bulk micro weights (sensory reservoirs, spiking motifs): ternary to INT4. Their errors are averaged over many synapses.
Static default 2: Activations and spike/state traffic: INT8 or FP8 E4M3; E5M2 for gradients and rarely large signals.
Static default 3: Time constants, gates, leak rates, LTC tau parameters: FP32. Small errors in tau shift the whole dynamical regime.
Static default 4: Accumulators (membrane potentials over long windows, eligibility traces, reward integrals): FP32 or posit32, with stochastic rounding if stored lower.
Static default 5: Homeostatic set points and slow integrators: FP64. These are few, long-lived and drift-sensitive.
Static default 6: Master copies for self-rewrite: FP32 shadow of any weight that the governor may modify (Section 6).

Adaptive precision trigger 1 (precision moves at run time): Shadow divergence: periodically run a cell at one rung higher on the same input and measure behavioural divergence; promote if divergence exceeds a budget, demote if it stays negligible.

Adaptive precision trigger 2 (precision moves at run time): Surprise: when a cell's prediction error spikes (novel environment, injury), temporarily promote its precision so learning is not swamped by quantisation noise; demote as surprise decays.

Adaptive precision trigger 3 (precision moves at run time): Energy budget: an organism-level energy variable (itself a causal part of the simulation) caps total bit-operations; the allocator solves a knapsack-like problem, maximising sum D(theta) * benefit subject to cost.
A useful developmental schedule (Recipe R8) starts the organism at high precision and anneals toward lower precision as structure stabilises, the reverse of the usual train-then-quantise pipeline.

Model-type allocation row 1: sub-problem character 'Sparse, event-like, energy-critical' -> preferred family sLTC (flagship), LIF, Izhikevich — why: events only; adaptive tau from LTC; reported energy savings.
Model-type allocation row 2: sub-problem character 'Rich transient features of a fast stream' -> preferred family Reservoir / LSM / ESN — why: fixed random dynamics, cheap linear readout.
Model-type allocation row 3: sub-problem character 'Smooth control with variable timescales' -> preferred family LTC / CfC / neural ODE — why: input-dependent time constants.
Model-type allocation row 4: sub-problem character 'Long sequences, memory compression' -> preferred family Selective SSM (Mamba), S4 — why: linear-time scan, selective retention.
Model-type allocation row 5: sub-problem character 'Prediction, imagination, planning' -> preferred family World model (RSSM, JEPA-style) — why: latent rollouts without acting.
Model-type allocation row 6: sub-problem character 'Pose, contact, rotation, body schema' -> preferred family Clifford / equivariant nets — why: group structure by construction.
Model-type allocation row 7: sub-problem character 'Episodic recall, pattern completion' -> preferred family Modern Hopfield, HDC — why: content addressing.
Model-type allocation row 8: sub-problem character 'Morphogenesis, tissue, growth' -> preferred family Neural cellular automata, PDE cells — why: local rules, global form.
Model-type allocation row 9: sub-problem character 'Slow physiology, mood, homeostasis' -> preferred family Low-dim ODE/DDE/fractional integrators — why: interpretable, stable, high precision.

sLTC as the flagship micro/meso block: the default choice for any sub-brain that is event-driven, energy-limited or a candidate for low precision; NESTOR-specific hypotheses (untested by the published work): sLTC cells tolerate ternary weights and INT8 state, their spikes are a natural S2S payload, and banks of sLTC cells with similar time constants are good DSD targets.
Allocation can be fixed by the designer, chosen by evolution (the model type is a gene), or learned by a router that instantiates candidate families in parallel and lets DSD merge the winners.

Interfaces: every port is typed by (algebra, shape, precision, clock, semantics tag); spikes, continuous states, latent caches and scalar neuromodulators are all legal port types; text tokens are not required anywhere.
Shared state (ii): global neuromodulators — a handful of FP32/FP64 scalars, e.g. 'arousal', 'reward prediction error', 'fatigue' — that multiply gains and plasticity rates everywhere.

Timescales: each cell runs on its own clock: fixed-step, event-driven, or adaptive-step (ODE solver). The runtime is a multi-rate scheduler: fast cells take many steps per slow step; slow cells see fast cells through time-aggregating adapters (rate, last value, leaky average, or a learned summariser); fast cells see slow cells as piecewise-constant or interpolated context.
items.criterion: Communication across a timescale boundary is always mediated, never a raw read of another cell's internal buffer.

items.text: Differential weights and biases: each weight may be stored as a base value plus differentials, w = w0 + dw(position) + dw(context) + dw(time); the base w0 can be shared across many synapses by DSD, while the small differentials are stored at low precision.

Placement manifold / differential spacing: every cell and unit has coordinates in a placement space (a 3D body frame, a sphere S2 or hypersphere, or a hyperbolic disc); wiring probability, conduction delay and plasticity rate are functions of placement distance — spacing is not cosmetic layout but a parameter that changes delays and coupling.
S2S precision mismatch rule (1): decode with the source's scale metadata (block scales, zero points) before projecting; never project raw integer codes.
S2S precision mismatch rule (2): project in an interchange precision at least as high as the higher of the two endpoints, BF16 by default and FP32 for channels into slow integrators.
S2S precision mismatch rule (3): re-quantise into the target's format with stochastic rounding so that repeated small updates are not rounded away.

S2S precision mismatch rule (4): monitor the channel's precision loss, the divergence between the fused result at interchange precision and at target precision, and let the allocator promote the channel if it is large.

S2S timescale mismatch rule 1: Fast to slow: aggregate (spike counts, exponential traces with time constant matched to the target, or a tiny learned summariser). Aliasing is the main risk; low-pass before downsampling.
S2S timescale mismatch rule 2: Slow to fast: hold (zero-order), interpolate, or send as a modulatory context rather than a driving input.
S2S timescale mismatch rule 3: Event-driven: send only when the source state changes by more than a threshold (delta coding), which also makes the channel sparse and cheap.

S2S timescale mismatch rule 4: Continuous-time targets (LTC, neural ODE/CDE): treat the incoming state as a control path X(t); neural controlled differential equations are a natural fit, since they consume irregularly sampled paths.

Precision per component: a multi-dimensional weight is a small vector of numbers, and each component, or each grade of a multivector, may have its own rung. A reasonable default, to be tested: scalar part at the highest precision (it sets overall gain), vector part one rung lower, bivector (rotation) part at a precision chosen by how finely orientation must be resolved, and higher grades lowest.

Alternative: store the weight in a polar form — magnitude at high precision and direction on a quantised sphere (e.g. a geodesic grid of 2^b points for b bits); ternary generalises to ternary per component (3^k states for k components) or to a small codebook of unit directions, a 'polyhedral' weight.
Tiers of rewrite authority: tier 0 (fast weights, bounded plasticity) acts freely within hard norm bounds.
Tiers of rewrite authority: tier 1 (weight deltas from hypernetworks or learned optimisers) requires sandbox verification.
Tiers of rewrite authority: tier 2 (structural changes, model-type swaps, DSD merges) requires verification plus a rate limit.
Invariants: spectral radius limits on recurrent matrices, bounds on time constants, homeostatic set-point protection (the FP64 homeostat cannot be rewritten by the cells it regulates), energy budget.

ChronoBlock-4 (CB4): a block-scaled 4-bit format with a temporal (spike-count) precision channel and a geometric grade map. A tensor is cut into blocks of 16 elements; each block stores a shared FP8 (E4M3) scale s_b, as in NVFP4, and a 2-bit mode tag mu_b; 16 element codes of 4 bits each; plus one tensor-level FP32 scale S.

CB4 element codes are interpreted according to the mode tag: FP4 mode (E2M1, as NVFP4); ternary-plus-time mode (2 bits ternary q in {-1, 0, +1} and a 2-bit temporal dither phase); grade mode (the 64 element bits are reallocated across two Cl(3,0) multivectors, e.g. scalar 6, each vector component 4, each bivector component 3, trivector 2 bits, totalling 58 bits plus spare).

CB4 decoded value of element i at time step t: x_i(t) = S * s_b * ( q_i + eps_b [ b_i(t) - 1/2 ] ), b_i(t) = 1[ (t + phi_i) mod L < r_i ], where q_i is the stored code, eps_b one unit in the last place for the block, phi_i the stored dither phase, r_i a residual rate; over an integration window of L steps the time average recovers sub-ULP resolution: precision grows with integration time, so a cell receives a 4-bit value per step but effectively more bits per window.

CB4 storage is 4 + (8 + 2)/16 ~ 4.63 bits per element, plus a negligible tensor scale, versus about 4.5 for NVFP4; the allocator flips one 2-bit tag per block, so adaptive precision costs no data movement.

CB4 cost: decoding needs a mode switch and a phase counter per block; on current hardware this would be emulated (no native support), so speed claims must be measured on custom kernels, FPGAs or neuromorphic hardware.
items.criterion: Specialist test (E11b): emulate CB4 against NVFP4, MXFP4, INT4 and ternary at matched bits per element on (i) weight storage of an sLTC network, (ii) multivector weights in a rotation task; measure accuracy versus integration window L and drift of slow integrators.

items.text: Spindle synapse cost per synapse: a pointer (12–16 bits for a library of 4k–64k rotors) plus a 3-component bivector at about 4 bits each, i.e. roughly 24–28 bits per synapse for a full 3D rotation and gain, with the distance computed from positions (cacheable); with CB4 storage, the differential lives in grade mode at 3–4 bits per component; the sandwich product costs on the order of tens of multiply–adds.

Spindle synapse: W_ij = g(d_H(p_i, p_j)) R_cij exp(-delta_ij/2), g(d) = exp(-d/lambda); delay dt_ij = d_H(p_i, p_j) / v_c — each synapse rotates a multivector signal, attenuates it by hyperbolic distance, and delays it by distance.

Frankenstein Prime: a CHIMERA unit whose input synapses are Spindle synapses and whose every stored tensor (W_in differentials, Xi, A, B, C, state checkpoints) is held in ChronoBlock-4; coupling (a): the CHIMERA step Delta also sets the CB4 integration window L (fast, salient moments get coarser but faster updates; quiet periods integrate more bits).

Recipe R1. Ternary sLTC cortex with an FP32 liquid thalamus. Bulk sensory and associative layers are sLTC units with ternary weights and INT8 membrane state, learning by neuromodulated STDP; a small CfC/LTC 'thalamus' at FP32 gates which spiking areas are active and sets their thresholds; S2S channels carry spike traces up and gain fields down.
items.criterion: Tests: whether a cheap bulk plus a precise router matches a uniform BF16 brain.

items.text: Recipe R2. Liquid reservoir with a Mamba narrator. An analog-noise or stochastic-bitstream liquid state machine turns raw sensory streams into rich transients; a selective SSM at FP8/BF16 reads the reservoir through an S2S random-feature projector and maintains a compressed long-horizon summary; only the readout and the SSM adapt.
items.criterion: Tests: whether a fixed, cheap, noisy front end plus selective memory is enough for foraging with long gaps between cues.

items.text: Recipe R3. Clifford body schema. A geometric-algebra network with rotor-valued weights (BF16 scalar/vector parts, INT4 bivectors) represents limb poses and contacts in Cl(3,0) or a projective algebra; a hypernetwork writes the weights of ternary spiking motor primitives from the current body schema.
items.criterion: Tests: sample efficiency on a morphologically variable body (limbs added/removed).

items.text: Recipe R4. Dream loop with an FP64 homeostat. A latent world model (RSSM style, BF16, posit16 latents) runs imagination rollouts on its own clock; a low-dimensional FP64 ODE homeostat holds energy, temperature and 'mood' set points and injects them as S2S context into imagined rollouts.
items.criterion: Tests: planning quality versus imagination horizon, and drift of the homeostat under precision changes.

items.text: Recipe R5. Fractal colony. Hundreds of identical micro-brains (neural cellular automaton cells at posit8) tile a body; DSD formalisations F3/F4 keep one canonical cell plus INT2 differentials per position; evolution acts on the canonical cell and the differential generator.
items.criterion: Tests: whether DSD keeps memory near-constant as the colony grows, and how much diversity is lost.

items.text: Recipe R6. Hub-and-sphere associative core. A modern Hopfield memory whose stored patterns live on a hypersphere, with LNS8 arithmetic, is the hub; hyperdimensional bipolar vectors (1 bit per component) bind context to items; fast weights store the last few minutes of episodes.
items.criterion: Tests: episodic recall under heavy noise and low precision.

items.text: Recipe R7. Event-driven sLTC-to-Mamba bridge. An sLTC front end emits events; an S2S delta-coded channel feeds them to a selective SSM whose step size is driven by event timing rather than a fixed clock; complex-valued weights in the bridge encode spike phase relative to a hub rhythm.
items.criterion: Tests: compute saved by event-driven updates versus fixed-step, at equal task performance, and whether the sLTC energy advantage reported in isolation survives inside a hybrid.

items.text: Recipe R8. Precision-annealing embryo. The organism is born with all cells at FP32 and quaternion-valued weights in its controller; as each cell's shadow divergence falls, the allocator demotes it rung by rung, potentially to ternary components, while DSD merges stabilised motifs; evolution selects the annealing schedule.
items.criterion: Tests: whether develop-then-compress beats train-low-precision-from-scratch.

items.text: Recipe R9. Differential twin. Two copies of one LTC (or sLTC) cell run in parallel, one at ternary and one at FP32; their difference is itself a signal, interpreted as a novelty or uncertainty detector; the difference drives neuromodulated plasticity and precision promotion.
items.criterion: Tests: whether twin disagreement predicts out-of-distribution inputs and errors.

items.text: Recipe R10. Fractional jet homeostat. Slow physiological variables follow fractional-order ODEs (learned alpha) with geometry-derived delays; each outputs a jet (x, x', x'', x(3)) at FP64, and complex-valued weights couple variables into damped oscillations; downstream controllers read jerk as a 'something changed' signal.
items.criterion: Tests: whether higher-derivative channels improve anticipation of regime shifts beyond what the level and trend give.

items.text: Design principle P1. Hard-wired and causal; nothing cosmetic. Every variable in a NESTOR brain must lie on a causal path to behaviour or to another causal variable; a 'mood' must change gains, thresholds, precision or plasticity; a placement coordinate must set delays or wiring.
items.criterion: A cosmetic-variable audit is run on every build, clamping each named variable and measuring the effect on behaviour; any variable with no measurable effect is flagged; labels in the code are never trusted as evidence of function; interventions are.

items.text: Design principle P2. Adaptive, reactive, responsive, dynamic. Structure, precision, model type, wiring and weights can all change at run time within governed bounds.
items.criterion: Reactive means a fast path exists from any sensor to some actuator without passing through slow cells; responsive means latency budgets are declared per cell and monitored.

items.text: Design principle P3. Omnitemporal. The framework supports many clocks at once (event-driven, fixed-step, adaptive-step), many timescales (sub-millisecond to lifetime), and many temporal operators (derivatives, fractional memory, delays, imagination rollouts into the future, replay of the past). Time is a typed property of every port.

Design principle P4. Omnimodal. Senses and actuators are just typed ports: spike trains, continuous fields, multivectors, images, audio, proprioception, chemical gradients. No modality is privileged and none is converted to tokens.

Design principle P5. Multiplatform. The cell contract is substrate-neutral: a cell can run on CPU, GPU, a neuromorphic chip, an analog accelerator or a microcontroller, provided it honours its port types and precision declarations; precision declarations double as portability declarations (a ternary/INT8 cell can be moved to an integer-only device).

Design principle P6. Fully observable, data exportable. Every cell emits a ledger Lambda: states (sampled or full), spikes, gates, precision rung history, S2S traffic, DSD merges and splits, self-rewrite events, energy use, and random seeds; export formats are open (Parquet/Arrow, HDF5/Zarr, NWB for spike data, JSON for configuration).
items.criterion: A run must be replayable from its ledger and seeds, which is why a small set of values is kept at FP64 even when the live organism does not need it.

items.text: Design principle P7. Reversible structure. Every structural operation (unfold, merge, rewrite, precision change) is logged with enough information to undo it.

Design principle P8. Speculation is labelled. Configuration files mark which components are established methods and which are experimental NESTOR proposals, so that results can be attributed correctly.

Experimental philosophy: no fixed grade thresholds or pass/fail cut-offs are used; every comparison is reported as an effect size with uncertainty (bootstrap confidence intervals over at least several independent seeds), against a stated baseline, with the comparisons declared before running; negative results are first-class outcomes.

Worlds: three generic test worlds of increasing difficulty: (W1) a 2D foraging arena with delayed cues and predators; (W2) a 3D articulated or soft-body locomotion world with variable morphology; (W3) a multi-organism ecology with resource cycles, where homeostasis and long-horizon memory matter.

Baselines: a monolithic BF16 recurrent controller (GRU/LSTM) of matched parameter count; a monolithic SSM; a uniform-precision version of each recipe; and the same recipe with all NESTOR-specific mechanisms disabled.
E1. Precision sensitivity map. For each tensor role (weights, activations, time constants, accumulators, homeostatic state), sweep the ladder rung by rung while holding others at FP32.
items.criterion: Measure behavioural divergence from an FP64 reference and task competence; output: an empirical version of Figure 2 for each model family.

items.text: E2. Adaptive versus static precision. Compare the shadow-divergence, surprise and energy-budget triggers against the best static allocation from E1.
items.criterion: Comparison at equal average bit-operations.

items.text: E2b. sLTC under NESTOR conditions. First reproduce the published sLTC vs LTC vs LSM comparison on an event-driven benchmark as a sanity check, then test sLTC at ternary/INT4/INT8 weights, sLTC as an S2S source, and DSD merging of sLTC banks.
items.criterion: Report energy proxies (synaptic events, bit-operations) and accuracy.

items.text: Ablation: uniform precision (each rung) — is heterogeneous precision better than the best single rung?
Ablation: freeze precision allocator — what does adaptivity add?
Metric — Fidelity: behavioural divergence from an FP64 reference run (e.g. action-distribution divergence, trajectory distance).
Metric — Efficiency: bit-operations, memory bytes (including DSD library), wall-clock and energy on target hardware, sample efficiency (episodes to competence).

Heptarch: functional arousal a, valence v and dominance d are carried as jets (a, a', a'', a(3)), estimated by state observers at a promoted ChronoBlock-4 rung, since each derivative order amplifies noise.
Heptarch upgrade U4 (Spindle): mechanical relaxation (tau ~ 1–10 s) for slow charge.
Heptarch upgrade U9 (Capacitor): fast, medium and slow metabolic homeostats; Supernova overdraws and Zenkai repays.
Frontier Sweep upgrade-map row (H-JEPA): make Chronoscope's horizons explicit JEPA levels (fast/medium/slow) with LongGame planning top-down; this matches the ChronoBlock-4 tiering.
Frontier Sweep F1 DASL cell: one unit — an sLTC soma fed by 4-8 dendritic branches; synapses on a branch have ternary weights (a sign and a mask).
items.criterion: Test / metric: in-episode adaptation speed vs CHIMERA-1; energy per tick; ternary-vs-FP accuracy on reflexes.

items.text: Frontier Sweep F2 VISC-Spindle: each synapse holds a hidden state s, a slow ferro-precision accumulator f, a mechanical-relaxation term m (tau 1-10 s) and a fatigue term z; each synapse has a finite write budget.
items.criterion: Test / metric: seconds-scale integration test (16 sub-threshold pulses cause a fire); recall stability after Supernova.

items.text: Frontier Sweep F3 Thermocore: a simulated sparse Ising lattice (16 neighbours, chromatic Gibbs updates); 2-8 chained denoising energy steps for Chronoscope's multimodal futures; annealing ternary Spindle weights.
items.criterion: Test / metric: sample quality vs steps; ternary training loss vs SGD baseline; Wildcard unpredictability per energy.
